Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

A great book is a book people have loved and argued about for a very long time. Some are hundreds of years old. Some are thousands! They tell of heroes and voyages, of clever questions, and of how people found out how the world works.
Great books can feel hard at first. The words may be old, and the sentences long. That is fine. You don't have to understand everything the first time. Nobody does.

items: Read with a grown-up. Take turns reading aloud, a page each.
Read a little at a time. Ten or fifteen minutes is plenty.
Tell it back. Close the book and say what happened, in your own words.
Ask a question. What surprised you? What would you have done?

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this: the tell-back game

Read one short part of a story with someone. Then close the book. Take turns telling it back, one sentence each, until you reach the end. Open the book and check: did you leave anything out? Then draw your favorite moment.
You don't have to understand it all the first time. Great books are meant to be read again and again, and they grow with you.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

A great book is one that is still worth reading long after it was written. It takes up questions people keep asking: what is just, what is true, how nature works, how to live. It rewards a second reading, and a third. And it has been part of a long conversation, with later writers answering, quarreling with or building on it.

The classic guide to reading such books is How to Read a Book by Mortimer J. Adler, first published in 1940 and rewritten with Charles Van Doren in 1972. It describes reading as an active skill that can be learned, and it is known for setting out levels of reading: the elementary level of reading the words, a quick inspectional look at a whole book, the slow, careful analytical reading of one book, and syntopical reading, which compares several books on one subject. It is well worth reading in full; your library will have it. What follows is our own advice, for families.

items: Choose well. Start with a work that matches your interests: a story (Homer, Shakespeare), a short argument (Plato's Apology), or a science classic with experiments you can try (Galileo, Faraday).
Pick a good translation. Many older translations are in the public domain and free. If one reads stiffly, try another.
Look the book over first. Read the title page, the contents and the first and last pages of a chapter or two. Find out when it was written and what was happening then.
Set a pace. Fifteen or twenty minutes a day goes a long way. The Harvard Classics Daily readings on this site take about that long.
Read it through once without stopping to look up every hard word or name. Mark what puzzles you and keep going. A whole book makes sense of its parts.
Read with a pencil. Underline key sentences, number the steps of an argument, write questions in the margin. In a library book, use sticky notes or a notebook.
Ask the author questions. Who is speaking, and to whom? What problem is the author trying to solve? What would they say to someone who disagreed? Where do you agree, and why?
Read aloud poems, plays and speeches. They were written to be heard.
Tell it back. After each sitting, say or write a few sentences about what you read. This is called narration, and it is one of the best ways to remember.
Talk about it. A book talk at dinner, with one question each, is a fine start. Give reasons, point to the page, and listen as carefully as you speak.
Be fair before you judge. Make sure you can state the author's view in a way the author would accept. Then say where you agree or disagree.
Keep a commonplace book. Copy out passages you want to keep. Many great readers did this.
Come back to it. A great book read at twelve and again at forty is two different books.

blocks.html: Bacon's point is that books ask for different kinds of reading. A great book belongs in his last group: it is worth reading wholly, with attention, and more than once.
Giving up because the first chapter is hard. Many great books start slowly, or start with the hardest part. Read on to the end once, then go back; the opening often makes sense only afterward.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Two kinds of reading. Most of what we read, we read for information: the news, a recipe, a manual. A great book asks something more of us. We read it to understand, which means following an argument we did not already know and could not have made ourselves. Adler's book makes a great deal of this difference, and it is the reason great books feel slow: understanding takes longer than collecting facts.

Reading across books. The highest level in Adler's scheme, syntopical reading, means putting several authors side by side on one question and working out where they agree and disagree. His Syntopicon, the index of ideas that fills the first two volumes of Great Books of the Western World, was built to make that kind of reading possible. Our own Great Ideas index does the same on a small scale for this ladder.

Translations. Most of the great books were written in Greek, Latin, Italian, French, German or Russian. Every translation is also an interpretation. Comparing two translations of one passage is a good way to see what the translator decided, and to get closer to the original.

Reading the old science books. Euclid, Galileo, Newton and Faraday are worth reading even though science has moved on. You see how a discovery was made, what the author had to argue against, and what the evidence looked like before anyone knew the answer. Where an old book got something wrong, the lesson on that rung says so.

Reading with children. The educator Charlotte Mason (1842–1923) built a whole way of schooling on reading good books and telling them back. Families who follow her, and many who don't, find that children can enjoy far more demanding books than we expect, as long as they hear them read well, a little at a time, and get to talk about them.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. What is a book you have read more than once? Was it different the second time?
  2. Bacon says some books should be tasted and some chewed and digested. Name a book of each kind.
  3. Is it better to read a hard book alone or with others? Why?
  4. What makes a book great: that it is old, that many people have read it, or something else?
  5. When you disagree with a book, how can you be sure you understood it first?
  6. Which great book would you like to read together first, and why?

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Imagine a conversation that has gone on for almost three thousand years. A poet in ancient Greece tells a story about a hero. Hundreds of years later, a philosopher asks whether that hero was really good. Another writer answers him. A scientist checks an old idea with a new experiment. Each one has read the ones before.
People call this the Great Conversation, and the books in it the great books. When you read one, you get to join in. You can agree, disagree, and ask your own questions.

🧩 Try this: a conversation chain

Sit in a circle. The first person asks a big question, like "What makes someone brave?" The next person gives an answer and one reason. The next person says what they think of that answer, and adds their own. Keep going around. You have just had a small great conversation!
This ladder is a climb through those books, one rung at a time. Every rung has a part just for young readers, like this one.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

The Great Books idea is simple to state. Some books take up the deepest questions people ask, they have shaped how later people thought, and they are worth reading in the original (or a faithful translation) rather than only in summaries. Read together, they form a long conversation across the centuries, which anyone who reads them can join.

blocks.cap: The Great Books idea in America: a short history
head: When
What happened
rows: At Columbia University, the English professor John Erskine begins his General Honors course, planned since 1917 and delayed by the First World War. Juniors and seniors read one classic a week, from Homer onward, and discuss it in seminar. Mortimer Adler was one of his students.
Early 1930s

Robert Maynard Hutchins, the young president of the University of Chicago, and Mortimer J. Adler, whom he brought there in 1930, teach a Great Books seminar together and argue for an education built on the classics.

St. John's College in Annapolis, Maryland, under Stringfellow Barr and Scott Buchanan, adopts a four-year program built almost entirely on the great books, with seminars, tutorials and laboratories in place of lectures and textbooks. A second campus opened in Santa Fe, New Mexico, in 1964.
The University of Chicago begins the Basic Program of Liberal Education for Adults, a four-year, non-credit course of weekly discussions of great books. It still runs today.
Hutchins and Adler start the Great Books Foundation, which helps adults and students run discussion groups all over the country.

Encyclopaedia Britannica publishes Great Books of the Western World in 54 volumes, with Hutchins as editor-in-chief and Adler as associate editor. Volume 1 is Hutchins' essay The Great Conversation, and volumes 2 and 3 are Adler's Syntopicon, an index of great ideas across the set.

The second edition, edited by Adler with Philip W. Goetz, grows to 60 volumes. It adds six volumes of 20th-century works, new translations, Voltaire's Candide, and four women authors (Jane Austen, George Eliot, Willa Cather and Virginia Woolf), and drops a few works, such as Apollonius on conic sections. This is the set this ladder follows.

blocks.html: Hutchins' opening essay argues, in his own words, that these books belong to everyone, not only to scholars, and that a free people needs citizens who can think through the great questions together. The essay is still under copyright, so we describe it rather than quote it; a library can lend you the set.

Arnold, writing in 1869, gave the idea its most famous phrase: "the best which has been thought and said." Notice what he says it is for: not to make us agree with the past, but to turn fresh thought on our own habits.

blocks.text: The case against a fixed list

blocks.html: The Great Books idea has always had critics, and a fair reader should know their arguments as well as the defenders' replies.

blocks.cap: Main criticisms and replies, stated fairly
head: Critics say
Defenders reply
rows: Any list reflects the people who chose it. The 1952 set had no women authors and almost no writers from outside Europe and North America.
The list is a starting point, not a fence. The 1990 edition added authors, and the conversation can welcome more; the test is the work's depth, not its author.
A list called "great" can be treated as beyond question, which is the opposite of what the authors themselves did.
The books disagree with each other constantly. Reading them teaches questioning, not obedience.
Reading old books without their history leads to misreading them.
History helps, and good teachers supply it, but the books can also be read for their arguments, which can be judged on their merits.
The 1952 set was sold door to door as a status symbol, and many sets sat unread. Critics such as Dwight Macdonald mocked the Syntopicon as a shortcut to culture.
However it was sold, the set put the originals in many homes and libraries, and discussion groups across the country read them.
Some works, especially in science, are out of date.
They show how knowledge was won, and the ideas they argue about are still with us.

blocks.html: Teddy Rook Book doesn't take a side in the argument over the canon. We follow the 1990 set because the owner of the set asked for it and because it is a good map of a long conversation. You are free to read beyond it, and we hope you will.

items: Every rung is one work (or one part of a long work) from the 60 volumes, in eras from the Greeks to the 20th century. Each rung shows its volume number, so you can find it on your shelf.
Three paths on every rung: for young readers (about 8 to 12), for teens and adults, and going deeper. Read the one that fits, or all three.

Short excerpts come only from translations old enough to be in the public domain, each with its source. Where no free English translation exists, we describe the work in our own words and tell you where to find it.

Practice checks what you learned: who wrote what, when, the main ideas, and for the science books the real math and physics. Pass a rung and it comes back for short reviews, like every ladder on this site.
Cross-links take you to the matching Physics, Astronomy, Math, Chemistry or Biology topics, and to the Harvard Classics Daily readings by the same author.
Rungs marked "being written" are on the way. The science books come first.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

An older shelf. The Great Books idea in America is older than Erskine's course. In 1909 and 1910, Charles W. Eliot, the former president of Harvard, published the Harvard Classics, a fifty-volume "five-foot shelf" meant to give a good liberal education to anyone who read fifteen minutes a day. Its reading guide is the basis of this site's Harvard Classics Daily, and many of its authors are on this ladder too.

Why "conversation"? The word fits because the books really do answer each other. Aristotle argues with Plato; Augustine answers the Roman historians; Galileo writes his dialogue against the followers of Aristotle; Rousseau answers Hobbes and Locke about the state of nature; Marx and Mill read Adam Smith. Our Great Ideas index lets you follow one idea through many of them.

The canon debates. In the 1980s and 1990s, American colleges argued hard about whether to require a list of Western classics, and if so which. Some writers defended a common core of reading as shared ground for citizens; others argued that a required list should include more voices, or that no single list should be required. Both sides often agreed that students should read difficult original works closely; they differed on which works, and why.

Where it lives today. Great-books programs still run in many forms: whole colleges like St. John's, honors programs and core curricula at many universities, adult reading groups, homeschool co-ops, and families reading at the kitchen table.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. If you could ask one question to a writer from long ago, who would it be and what would you ask?
  2. Why might it matter to read a book itself, rather than a summary of it?
  3. What makes a good conversation? What makes a bad one?
  4. Should there be a list of books everyone reads? What would you put on it, and who should decide?
  5. Arnold says reading the best that has been thought should change our own habits of thought. Has a book ever changed your mind?
  6. What is one book from your family or culture that you would add to the conversation?

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Mortimer Adler was born in New York City in 1902. He left school at fourteen to work as a copy boy at a newspaper. Then he found the books of the great thinkers, and he loved them so much that he spent the rest of his long life reading them, teaching them and helping other people read them too.

Adler had a giant idea. He wanted to make a map of the big ideas in all the great books. If you wondered, "What did the great writers think about courage?", the map would show you where each of them talked about it, book by book and page by page.
He and a team of readers worked for years to make it. It is called the Syntopicon, which means "a collection of topics," and it fills the first two volumes of the set this ladder follows.

🧩 Try this: make your own idea map

Pick one big idea, like courage, friendship or home. Think of three stories or books you know. Where does the idea show up in each one? Write the idea at the top of a page and the three places under it. Now you have made a tiny Syntopicon!

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Adler grew up in New York, left high school at fourteen to work at the New York Sun, and took classes at Columbia University, where John Erskine's General Honors seminar on the classics shaped his life. Though he never finished high school, he earned a PhD in 1928, taught at Columbia, and in 1930 went to the University of Chicago at the invitation of its president, Robert Maynard Hutchins.

items: At Chicago, he and Hutchins taught the great books in seminars, and in 1946 and 1947 they helped start the Basic Program for adults and the Great Books Foundation.
He was associate editor of the first edition of Great Books of the Western World (1952) and made its Syntopicon. He was editor-in-chief of the second edition (1990).
In 1952 he founded the Institute for Philosophical Research, and he led seminars on the great books at the Aspen Institute for many years.
As chairman of Britannica's board of editors, he planned the 1974 edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica.
In the 1980s he led the Paideia project, which asked schools to teach every child through a mix of direct teaching, coaching and Socratic seminars.
He wrote more than fifty books, many for general readers.

blocks.html: An ordinary index tells you where a word appears in one book. The Syntopicon is an index of ideas across a whole library. Adler and his editors chose about a hundred great ideas (102 in the 1952 edition) and, over most of a decade, with a team of readers, went through every work in the set to record where each idea is discussed.

Each idea has its own chapter, and each chapter has five parts: an introductory essay by Adler on the idea and its history; an outline of topics, which breaks the idea into narrower questions; the references, which list, for each topic, the passages in the set by volume and page; cross-references to related ideas; and a list of additional readings outside the set. The 1990 edition added references to the new 20th-century volumes.
The Syntopicon makes syntopical reading possible: putting many authors side by side on one question, so you can see where they agree, where they disagree, and why.

items: Start with a question you care about, such as whether a law can be unjust, or what light is.
Find the idea it belongs to, and read Adler's essay for an overview.
Choose a topic in the outline that fits your question, and look up the passages listed for it.
Read them in order of time, from the oldest to the newest, taking notes on each author's answer.
Compare the answers in your own words, and decide what you think.

blocks.title: A syntopical reading, in miniature
blocks.q: Our own example: you want to know what the great writers thought about whether the Earth moves.
steps: On this ladder, the idea is The heavens and the planets. It lists the rungs that take up the question.
Read in order: Aristotle's On the Heavens (a still Earth at the center), Ptolemy's Almagest, Copernicus's On the Revolutions, Kepler, Galileo, then Newton's Principia.
For each, write one sentence: what does the author claim, and what is the main reason given?
Compare: which reasons were about observations, which about mathematics, and which about physics?
blocks.a: You have traced one question through two thousand years, the way the Syntopicon was meant to be used.

blocks.html: Adler's books are still under copyright, so we describe them here and link to library listings. Many public libraries have them.

blocks.cap: A selection of Mortimer Adler's books for general readers
head: Book
What it is
rows: How to Read a Book (1940; revised with Charles Van Doren, 1972)
The classic guide to active reading, from the first look at a book to comparing many books on one subject.
Philosopher at Large (1977)
His autobiography, including the story of the great books programs and the Syntopicon.
Aristotle for Everybody (1978)
Aristotle's main ideas, explained for readers who have never studied philosophy.
How to Think About God (1980)
A philosopher's case, made by reason alone, on the question of God's existence.
Six Great Ideas (1981)
Six ideas he thought every citizen should think about: truth, goodness and beauty, and liberty, equality and justice.
The Paideia Proposal (1982)
A short plan for schooling the same for all children, built on seminars and coaching as well as lessons.
How to Speak, How to Listen (1983)
A companion to How to Read a Book, on speeches, conversation and discussion.
Ten Philosophical Mistakes (1985)
Errors he believed modern philosophy made, and how to correct them.
We Hold These Truths (1987)
The ideas behind the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.
How to Think About the Great Ideas (2000)
Short chapters drawn from his television discussions of the great ideas.

blocks.html: Inspired by the Syntopicon, this ladder has its own Great Ideas index. It is much smaller and simpler, and it is ours: about sixty ideas, named and grouped in our own way, each listing the rungs on this ladder that take it up. It grows as new rungs are built. It is not the Syntopicon's list, and it does not try to replace it; for passage-by-passage references, the Syntopicon itself is the tool to use.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Why a list of ideas at all? Adler believed that the great authors, for all their differences, were talking about the same few great questions, and that showing this would invite readers into the conversation instead of leaving them lost in sixty volumes. Critics replied that any such list fixes the questions in advance, and that the meaning of an idea changes from age to age. Dwight Macdonald's famous 1952 review in The New Yorker mocked the whole project as a shortcut to culture.

How an index changes reading. Before the Syntopicon, a reader who wanted to compare twenty authors on justice had to find the passages alone. The index made comparison easy, but some readers worried that it would tempt people to jump between passages without reading the whole works.

Topics across ladders. A modern version of the same idea is the hyperlink. On this site, the "Read the source" cards on Physics, Math, Chemistry and Biology topics point back to the great books where those ideas began, and each rung points forward to the topics that grew out of it.

Making your own. Many serious readers keep their own index: a notebook with an idea at the top of each page and references below. Over years it becomes a map of your own reading, and it is the best way to remember what you read.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. If you made a map of ideas from the books you have read, which three ideas would be on it?
  2. Is it better to read a whole book, or to read what many books say about one idea? When is each better?
  3. Adler worked for years on an index so that other people could read better. What would you work that hard on?
  4. Which idea in our Great Ideas index would you like to follow first, and why?
  5. Can a list of "great ideas" ever be complete? What might be missing?
  6. What question would you like to ask several great writers at once?
